title: Cleaning chemicals and COSHH
siteNotes: Which cleaning chemicals and products the venue actually uses in each department (your manager will show you).
Where the safety data sheets are kept and how to get to them quickly.
Which gloves and eye protection to wear for each product, and where the PPE is stored.
Exactly how to dilute each product, and which dispensing systems or measures are used.
Where chemicals are stored and who has keys, plus where eye wash and first aid kit are and who the first aiders are.
Who to report spills, splashes and fumes to, and how they are recorded.
legalNotes: Employers must give information, instruction and training to anyone exposed to hazardous substances, including what to do in an accident such as a spill, and give access to safety data sheets: COSHH 2002 and HSE training guidance (https://www.hse.gov.uk/coshh/basics/training.htm). Verified.
COSHH covers cleaning and maintenance staff who may meet hazardous substances (same HSE page). Verified.

Labels and hazard pictograms: the GB CLP Regulation sets the label rules (the GHS system). The HSE chemicals labelling page could not be loaded, so the pictogram meanings are well-known, but I could not confirm them against the HSE page. Please check against https://www.hse.gov.uk/chemical-classification/labelling-packaging/ .

Mixing products: the warning that bleach must never be mixed with acids or other products is standard manufacturer and safety data sheet advice (bleach plus acid gives off chlorine gas). Not quoted from HSE in this session.

First aid for splashes and fumes: general advice (rinse eyes and skin with plenty of water, get to fresh air, check the product label and safety data sheet, get medical help). The product's own safety data sheet takes priority. Not verified against HSE text in this session.
Decanting only into properly labelled containers is good practice based on the CLP labelling rules; not verified against a specific HSE page.
PPE must be provided and used where the risk assessment says so: Personal Protective Equipment at Work Regulations 1992 (not re-checked here).

Review 6 Oct 2026: nhs.uk/conditions/eye-injuries says that for a strong chemical in the eye (such as oven cleaner or bleach) call 999 or go to A&E, keep rinsing with water while waiting and take the container. The NHS page gives no fixed rinse time for chemicals; other eye-care sources say at least 15 to 20 minutes, so no number is taught and the product's safety data sheet takes priority. Slide and check wording extended to 'keep rinsing' and 'call 999 or A&E for a strong chemical'. Pictogram meanings (flame, skull and crossbones, corrosion, exclamation mark, health hazard, environment) and the red-bordered diamond format are the standard GB CLP/GHS pictograms; still not checked against the HSE labelling page. Whether employers must give workers 'access' to safety data sheets: COSHH reg. 12 requires information, instruction and training, and suppliers must provide SDSs to the employer; the session's wording ('must give staff access') is HSE-style good practice stated slightly firmly, so Ward Hadaway may wish to confirm.

cards.title: Cleaning chemicals and COSHH
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- read a label and know where to find the safety data sheet
- use products safely and never mix them
- act fast after a splash, fumes or a spill

cards.title: Cleaning products can hurt you
cards.body:
Many everyday products can burn skin, damage eyes or make you ill if you breathe the fumes. COSHH is the law that says you must be told about those risks and shown how to stay safe.

> If you use a chemical at work, you have the right to be trained on it first.

items.title: Lungs
items.text: Fumes and sprays can cause breathing problems.

cards.title: Read the label every time
cards.body:
The label tells you what the product is and what danger it carries. Warning pictograms are diamonds with a red border. Learn what they mean.

**Your manager will show you** which products the venue uses.

items.title: Flame
items.text: Flammable. Keep away from heat and sparks.

items.title: Skull
items.text: Toxic. Can poison if swallowed, breathed or touched.

items.title: Corrosion
items.text: Burns skin and eyes, can damage metal.

items.title: Exclamation mark
items.text: Irritant or harmful in lesser ways.

items.title: Health hazard
items.text: Serious long-term harm, such as to the lungs.

items.title: Environment
items.text: Harmful to water life. Never pour away carelessly.

cards.title: The full story is in the data sheet
cards.body:
A safety data sheet (SDS) covers hazards, handling, first aid, spill clean-up and storage for one product. You must be able to get to it.

- Check the SDS before using a new product
- **Your manager will show you** where the data sheets are kept

items.title: Read the label
items.text: Pictograms and wording on the container.

items.title: Check the SDS
items.text: Find the product's sheet before first use.

items.title: Wear the PPE
items.text: The gloves and eye protection it names.

items.title: Use as directed
items.text: Follow the instructions on the label.

cards.title: Never mix. Never decant.
cards.body: Mixing products can create dangerous gas. Bleach mixed with acid or another product is one of the worst examples.

left.title: Do
items: Use one product at a time

right.title: Do not
items: Mix bleach with acid or other products
Pour into water bottles or food and drink containers

cards.title: PPE and storage
cards.body:
Wear the protection your training says for that product, typically gloves and eye protection. Check it is clean and undamaged before use.

Store chemicals where your manager has shown you, closed, labelled and away from food.

cards.title: Splash, fumes or spill
cards.body: Act quickly and get help. Always check the label or data sheet for the product's own advice.

items.title: Spill
items.text: Keep others away, tell your supervisor, clean up only if trained.

items.title: Skin splash
items.text: Rinse with plenty of water and tell someone.

items.title: Eye splash
items.text: Rinse with plenty of water at once and keep rinsing. Call for help.

items.title: Fumes or feeling unwell
items.text: Get to fresh air, warn others, get help.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Read the label and know where the data sheet is
- Never mix products, especially bleach
- Dilute only as instructed and never decant into unlabelled or food containers
- Wear the right gloves and eye protection
- Report every spill, splash and fume straight away

cards.q: A toilet is badly stained. You have a bleach-based cleaner and a descaler. What is safest?
options: Use both together for a stronger clean
Use one only, then rinse it away well
Pour the descaler first, then add bleach on top
Mix them in a bucket with hot water
cards.why: Never mix products. Bleach combined with acid can release harmful gas. Use one as directed and rinse well.

cards.q: It is fine to pour a cleaning product into an empty water bottle if you know what is in it.
cards.why: Someone else may drink it. Chemicals stay in their original, labelled containers.

cards.q: A product splashes into your eye while you are cleaning. What do you do first?
options: Wipe it with your sleeve and carry on cleaning
Rinse the eye with lots of water and shout for help
Wait to see whether it stings
Finish the room first, then tell your supervisor later
cards.why: Eye splashes need immediate rinsing with plenty of water, and help. Keep rinsing, take the container to hospital, and call 999 or go to A&E for a strong chemical. Delay can make the damage worse.

cards.q: Which TWO places tell you how to handle a product and what to do if things go wrong?
options: The container label
A colleague's memory
The safety data sheet
The brand's advert
A guess based on the smell
cards.why: The label and the safety data sheet carry the hazards, protection and first aid. Smell and memory are not reliable.

cards.q: You find a bottle with no label under a sink. What should you do?
options: Sniff it to work out what it is
Use it, as it is probably the usual cleaner
Leave it alone and tell your manager
Tip it down the drain
cards.why: An unlabelled chemical is an unknown hazard. Do not use, smell or dispose of it yourself. Report it.

cards.q: A red-bordered diamond on a label shows a skull and crossbones. What does it warn?
options: The product is toxic and can poison
The product is only a mild irritant
The product is flammable
The product is harmless to water life
cards.why: The skull means toxic. Check the label and data sheet before you use it.

cards.q: The label says to dilute one part product to twenty of water. You are in a hurry. What do you do?
options: Add a bit extra for a stronger clean
Dilute only as instructed, even when busy
Guess from the last time you did it
Pour it in neat and wipe quickly
cards.why: Dilute only as instructed. Stronger is not safer or better, and can harm you or surfaces.

cards.q: Safety data sheets are only for managers and do not need to be available to cleaning staff.
cards.why: Employers must give staff access to the data sheets for products they use.

cards.q: Fumes from a product leave you dizzy in a small bathroom. What is the first thing to do?
options: Open a window and keep working
Spray air freshener to mask it
Stop, get to fresh air and tell someone
Finish the room, then take a break
cards.why: Leave the area for fresh air and get help. Check the label for the product's advice.

cards.q: A glove with a small split is fine for a short cleaning job.
cards.why: Damaged PPE does not protect you. Swap it before starting.
